name: Emeka Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I'm on an overhead crew in the northern suburbs for one of the big private electricity companies. We do new connections for houses, swap old transformers, and when a storm comes through we're out restoring power until it's done, sometimes eighteen hours. I'm an apprentice, second year, so Marco, the journeyman I'm paired with, does the hard bits on the live line and I set up, rig, and learn by watching his hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it at 43?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a forklift at a big distribution warehouse for twelve years, and in 2023 they put in the automatic shuttles and cut the night shift in half. I took the redundancy money and the company here had an apprenticeship scheme for older starters, so I went for it. What I like is that nobody can send a power line to another country, and what wears me out is being the slow one, Marco is patient but I can see him waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that noise for not much. At work we'd joke about it at lunch, Marco would say his phone still can't spell his name. I'd probably post a meme in the union group chat and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good news, it means the next ten years look like I planned. I get my ticket, I get journeyman pay, and Ines and I can stop doing sums every month. I've been pushed out by machines once, so I'd be glad to have a quiet decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the plan. Finish the apprenticeship in two years, keep using the chatbot now and then to explain the bits of the safety code I don't follow, and keep putting about two hundred a month into savings. Maybe in year two we'd finally fix the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat even, like when the forecast says storm and it just rains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chatbot for the safety code. How does that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in the section and ask it to explain it like I'm new, because I am new. Then I check it with Marco, because the bot was wrong once about clearance distances and he nearly took my head off. It's a helper, not the teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay keeping up with prices, same as always. And whether the company sells off our depot to some contractor, which has nothing to do with AI. That's the stuff I'd actually be talking to the union about.

S0.say: There you go, all that noise for not much. I'd joke about it at lunch and post a meme in the union group chat, and that would be it.
S0.think: For me it's good news, because the next ten years look like I planned: ticket, journeyman pay, less monthly worry. I've been pushed out by machines once already, so a quiet decade would suit me.
S0.do: Keeps following his plan to finish the apprenticeship in two years, using a chatbot now and then to explain the safety code and checking it with his journeyman. Keeps saving about two hundred a month and plans to fix the bathroom in year two.
S0.feel: Calm, even a bit flat, like a storm warning that turns out to be rain.
S0.quote: It's a helper, not the teacher.
S0.fieldNote: Having been replaced by warehouse shuttles once, he hears this picture as permission to follow his plan. He uses AI in a careful, practical way and double-checks it with his journeyman after one bad answer. His real background worries are pay and outsourcing, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen this film before, at the warehouse, and the workers who did okay were the ones whose union got in early. So I'd be telling the lads, get the deal written down now, before the new kit turns up. Online I'd share stories from people it's already happened to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I don't think it takes my job, not this one. Climbing poles in the rain and working on a live line is not where they'll start. What I think it does is change the job around me, drones doing patrols, software deciding which jobs come first, and I need to be the apprentice who's comfortable with all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd sign up for whatever drone or digital training the company offers, because last time I waited and it cost me. I'd go to union meetings more, not just read the chat. And I'd keep the bathroom money in the bank for another year, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I know the shape of it this time. Last time it came out of nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said last time you waited and it cost you. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the warehouse they offered a course on running the new shuttle system and I thought, nah, that's for the young ones. Six months later the three guys who did the course kept their jobs and I was carrying a box out to my car. I'm not doing that twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi, who's 14?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn how things work, not just how to use them. He wants to be a game designer, which is fine, but I'd say take the electrics module at school too. Hands and head, both.

S1.say: I've seen this film before at the warehouse, and the workers who did okay were the ones whose union got in early. Get the deal written down now, before the new kit turns up.
S1.think: I don't think it takes this job, because live-line work in the rain isn't where they'll start. But it will change everything around me, and I need to be the apprentice who's comfortable with drones and scheduling software.
S1.do: Signs up for any drone or digital training the company offers within the first few months. Goes to union meetings in person rather than just reading the chat, and holds the bathroom money in savings for another year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but steadier than last time because he recognises the pattern.
S1.quote: Six months later the three guys who did the course kept their jobs and I was carrying a box out to my car.
S1.fieldNote: His past redundancy is the key to him: it taught him both to trust the union and not to refuse training. He is steady rather than eager, waiting for proof, but this time the proof is his own history. The advice to his son about hands and head was heartfelt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the warehouse all over again but for everyone at once, and that's not something any one company should be allowed to do. I'd say the government has to step in, put a tax on the robots and pay people while they adjust. I'd be marching, and I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is my worst nightmare. I'd be halfway through being a lineworker, it's the second career I started because the first one got automated, and now it's gone before I've even finished. I don't think there's a third career for me at 45 if robots can do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the bathroom, stop any extras, and put every bit into savings the week it was announced. I'd talk to Ines about her pharmacy hours, maybe she goes full-time while it lasts. I'd be at the union meetings pushing for a guaranteed income scheme, and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being kicked in the same bruise twice. Angry and very tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what would you do differently in the time before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There isn't really time to train for anything, so I'd use it to save and to get organised with other people. I'd try to get every hour of overtime on storm jobs, because that's where the money is. Two years is enough to see it, not enough to dodge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ines works in a pharmacy. Would you worry about her too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than she does. She says people want a person to talk to about their medicine, but robots that can do anything can talk too. If we both lost work in the same year, we'd have about four months of savings, and then I don't know.

S2.say: This is the warehouse all over again, but for everyone at once, and no company should be allowed to do that. The government has to tax the robots and pay people while they adjust.
S2.think: Two years is my worst nightmare: linework is the second career I started because the first got automated, and it would be gone before I finished. I don't think there's a third career for me at 45.
S2.do: Stops the bathroom work and all extras and moves every spare amount into savings the week it is announced. Asks his partner about going full-time while she can, pushes his union for a guaranteed income scheme and writes to his MP for the first time.
S2.feel: Angry and very tired, like being kicked in the same bruise twice.
S2.quote: Like being kicked in the same bruise twice.
S2.fieldNote: This picture reopens his warehouse redundancy, and that history makes it much worse than for someone without it. He turns to policy and collective action, not personal reinvention, because he sees no time to retrain. He did the household maths out loud: about four months of savings if both incomes went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, which is enough to get the rules right if people wake up now. I'd push the union nationally to make it a big issue, retraining paid by the companies, a share of the savings. I'd be the guy at the barbecue who won't stop talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd get my ticket and maybe three years as a journeyman. That's more money in the bank and more say at work. I'd still be in trouble when it arrives, but not on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship first. Then I'd go for the company's robotics maintenance course, if they have one, because someone has to fix the robots and I'd rather be that guy than the guy they replace. I'd save hard in years three to five, maybe pay a chunk off the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious I can work with. Like the night before an exam you've studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the robots. How sure are you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, honestly. If the robots can do anything, maybe they fix each other. But for a few years someone has to be on site, and I'd rather be standing there with a toolbag than sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, we'd go down to one. Ines would hate it, she does the school run. Then the kids' extra clubs, and Ada would cry about football, but she'd get over it.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get the rules right if people wake up now. I'd push the union nationally for company-paid retraining and a share of the savings, and I wouldn't stop talking about it.
S3.think: With five years I'd get my ticket and maybe three years as a journeyman, which means more savings and more say. I'd still be in trouble when it arrives, but not on the floor.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, then takes any robotics maintenance course the company offers so he can fix machines rather than be replaced by them. Saves hard in years three to five and pays a chunk off the mortgage.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a workable way, like the night before an exam he has studied for.
S3.quote: I'd rather be standing there with a toolbag than sitting at home.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him enough room to plan a step sideways into robot maintenance, while staying honest that it may not last. He keeps a strong collective streak alongside his personal plan. The cuts he named, one car and the kids' clubs, show how close to the line the household runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disgrace if we waste it. I'd want the union and the government sitting down now, planning who gets retrained and who gets paid. I'd say it calmly, though, because ten years gives you time to be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I'm properly established, I'd have eight years as a lineworker and I'd be 53. Maybe I'd ride it out to something like early retirement with support, maybe I'd move into overseeing robots. I don't know which, but I'd have choices, and last time I had none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the ticket and get good at the job for the first few years. Around year four or five I'd start the robotics or controls training at night, slowly, the way I did my apprenticeship theory. And I'd tell Tobi and Ada to pick courses that keep a door open, and help pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade really change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choices. With two years I'm just reacting, like at the warehouse. With ten I get to decide, and that's the difference between being replaced and moving on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Marco about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him, yeah, he'd laugh and say he'll be retired and fishing by then. He's 59, so for him ten years is perfect. For me it's just enough.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift if we use it and a disgrace if we waste it. The union and the government should sit down now and plan who gets retrained and who gets paid.
S4.think: Ten years means I'm established, 53 with eight years as a lineworker, and I'd have choices about riding it out or moving into overseeing robots. Last time I had no choices at all.
S4.do: Finishes his ticket and builds skill in the first few years, then starts robotics or controls training at night around year four or five. Steers his children toward courses that keep options open and helps pay for them.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but mostly fine, and able to sleep.
S4.quote: With ten I get to decide, and that's the difference between being replaced and moving on.
S4.fieldNote: The decade turns him from someone things happen to into someone who decides, which is exactly what he lacked at the warehouse. His plans are gradual and proven-first, in line with his steady nature. His journeyman, close to retirement, sees the same decade as perfect timing, which he noted with some envy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would be my second career wiped out before I'd finished starting it. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the companies that save the money, and training offered early, before the jobs go, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many times a person can start over. I did it once at 41 and it took everything we had, the redundancy money, Ines's patience, my knees. I'd do it again if I had to, but people should know it's not free.

headlineQuote: I did it once at 41 and it took everything we had, the redundancy money, Ines's patience, my knees.
portrait: Emeka Petrov is a 43-year-old second-year lineworker apprentice on an overhead crew for a large private electricity company, after losing his warehouse forklift job to automation in 2023. He lives with his partner Ines, a pharmacy technician, and two children, with a mortgage and a few months of savings. He is pro-union and steady with technology, using a chatbot carefully to study and checking it with his journeyman. He is calm if AI stalls, uneasy but prepared with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because it would wipe out a second career. Longer warning times give him what he lacked last time: choices.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his second career would be wiped out before he had finished starting it.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while people retrain, paid for by the companies that save the money, and training offered before the jobs go rather than after.
